overview: This entry covers British-administered Uganda in the early twentieth century. Its population included several kingdoms and many other communities; Buganda was one part of the protectorate. Agreements, taxes and land arrangements changed political power, while farmers, teachers, traders and writers shaped everyday life under colonial rule.

periods.title: Agreements and colonial administration
periods.summary: The 1900 agreement defined British overrule and relations with Buganda, rather than making all Uganda one kingdom.

periods.title: Schools, crops and unequal representation
periods.summary: Technical education and cotton farming expanded, while the colonial council excluded most of the population.

periods.title: Later route to independence
periods.summary: The map interval ends before colonial rule did; independence came in October 1962.

items.text: The Legislative Council created in 1920 initially consisted entirely of Europeans. An Asian member joined in 1926, but the first African representatives were admitted only in 1945. A council could make decisions about people who had no representative of their own within it.

In Lango, farmers already grew sesame for trade with Bunyoro before cotton became important. John Tosh’s historical study argues that available household labour and competing crops mattered alongside colonial pressure: farmers were weighing what their time and land could produce.

Langi farmers expanded cotton cultivation in the early 1920s as the sesame market weakened and cotton prices improved. Growing an export crop involved choices about food security and seasonal work, not simply accepting a crop because an official recommended it.

A photograph preserved at Cambridge shows Ugandan workers at a cotton ginnery, operating machines that separated fibre from seeds. It makes an otherwise abstract export industry visible as a workplace. The catalogue page does not establish the photograph’s exact date.

Makerere opened in 1922 as a technical school with fourteen day students studying carpentry, building and mechanics. Its beginnings involved making and repairing useful things, rather than the many university subjects offered there later.

Makerere subsequently added medical care, agriculture, veterinary science and teacher training. These subjects connected classroom learning to treating people, caring for livestock, growing crops and teaching another generation; the institution developed beyond its original workshop courses.

“Ebifa mu Buganda” means “News in Buganda”. This is the Luganda title of a monthly periodical published from January 1907, using the Latin alphabet. The short sample follows the title recorded by the editors of Apolo Kivebulaya’s surviving writings.

Kivebulaya wrote about the consequences of fixing the border between British and Belgian territories. His articles show that African writers discussed how imperial boundaries affected local communities; they were participants in political debate, not merely subjects described by foreign officials.

Luganda periodicals also carried poems, proverbs, obituaries and discussions of religious and social life. Surviving copies in Ugandan collections let historians hear some educated local voices, while remembering that mission-supported newspapers did not represent every belief or household.

Sleeping-sickness campaigns changed where people could live around Lake Victoria. Colonial authorities forced communities away from affected shores and planned new settlements. Historian Kirk Hoppe connects these measures with long-term loss of access to land as well as attempts to control disease.

Restrictions also affected fishing, hunting and collecting firewood. For families who depended on the lake, disease control could mean losing food and income. Some residents resisted or returned secretly, showing the difference between an official plan and the choices people made to survive.

Medical authorities did not all agree about disease control. Environmental clearance and treatment programmes reflected competing priorities, limited knowledge and different colonial systems. A public-health campaign could therefore combine useful investigation with coercive policies that harmed the people it claimed to protect.

ending.text: British protectorate rule ended with Uganda’s independence on 9 October 1962. The imported 1938 endpoint marks a map interval, not the country’s disappearance. Its communities and institutions continued through the difficult transition to an independent state.
